One year ago, while gathering to worship, parishioners at the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in Grand Blanc suffered an unimaginable terror attack. I join the community in remembering the four victims, extending our prayers to their families and fellow congregants, and standing with the community as we remember the tragedies of that day.

Today, we also honor the heroic first responders who were on the scene in a matter of seconds. The remarkable speed and decision-making of our 911 dispatchers, law enforcement officers, firefighters, and paramedics saved lives.

In the days, weeks, and months since, neighbors have come together to grieve, heal, and find the light under the motto, “Grand Blanc, Better Together.” In the wake of an unimaginable tragedy, the Church and its community have shown us the power of faith and hope. As they break ground tonight, all of mid-Michigan will be behind them with love and support.

In my speech, I celebrated those courageous Bay Area Chinese-Americans—such as Wong Kim Ark, Mary Tape, and Lee Yick—who fought to ensure that America kept its commitment to our Constitution.

Thank you to Gerrye Wong and generations of community leaders who keep this history alive.

ROAD TO 250: Founders Close to Home

Before Roslyn was Roslyn, it was Hempstead Harbor — and Hendrick Onderdonk helped shape the community we know today.

Onderdonk settled here in 1752, operated the local grist mill and built Long Island’s first paper mill in 1773. During the Revolution, his property experienced the hardships of the British occupation, and his paper mill was part of a network used to pass secret wartime messages.

Years later, on April 24, 1790, President George Washington stopped at Onderdonk’s home during his tour of Long Island and wrote about his thriving mills.

More than 235 years later, the house where Washington stopped still stands on Old Northern Boulevard in Roslyn — today home to Hendrick’s Tavern.

It’s a place many of us know, with a history we may not: another reminder that the story of America’s founding is also part of our own local history.

ROAD TO 250: Founding Stories Close to Home

You don’t have to travel far to find a connection to America’s founding.

In 1790, President George Washington stopped in what is now Roslyn to visit Hendrick Onderdonk, a prominent local businessman who operated a grist mill and built Long Island’s first paper mill.

Onderdonk and his family had lived through the British occupation of Long Island, and his paper mill was part of a network used to carry secret messages during the Revolution.

The best part? The house where Washington stopped is still there today — now Hendrick’s Tavern on Old Northern Boulevard.

Our local history is American history.
